signals.title: Introducing Inkling 2 Mini - Thinking Machines Lab
signals.excerpt:
Nov 20, 2026

Today we are releasing Inkling 2 Mini, a fast, powerful model that’s small enough to run on your laptop.

Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality. Inkling 2 Mini leads every open-weights model with less than 100B total parameters on benchmarks such as DeepSWE v1.1 (48.2%) and Vals Index v2.2 (46.5%). It runs faster than similarly performing models as well.

...

Reported coding scores for models under 100B total parameters. The green line is the frontier with Inkling 2 Mini, the dashed line the frontier without it, and the shading the ground it adds. Decoding speed is a theoretical ceiling at 614 GB/s with BF16 weights and batch size one, including repeated reads across loops. Evaluation setups vary by model.

Inkling 2 Mini is a Mixture-of-Experts model with 26.4B total parameters, 3.4B active, and 5.4B weight activations per token to account for looping. Looping allows the model to reason longer without writing its reasoning down, which matters for monitoring: our ability to oversee and understand what the model does by reading its chain of thought (CoT).

We measured the impact of looping on both performance and monitorability with Inkling 2 Mini and a research-specific variable-loop variant we are releasing alongside it. The variable-loop model’s no-CoT time horizon improved from 16 seconds at one pass to 37 seconds with three, and its performance on a benchmark of serial reasoning kept improving out to ten loops—twice as many as it was trained with. The model’s chain of thought grew shorter with more loops but stayed legible throughout. The model didn’t trend higher on tests of agentic sabotage as loops were added.

We’re excited to offer some of the first models with looped architecture available to researchers. The variable-loop model was used for our monitorability experiments as it allows for cleaner comparisons between different looping depths.

Most of Inkling 2 Mini’s weights were trained and are deployed natively in NVFP4, with the last four layers in MXFP8. The total memory footprint of Inkling 2 Mini is ~20GB, allowing it to run on local devices such as consumer laptops and desktop AI computers.

...

Inkling 2 Mini is released with open weights and is available on Tinker today for inference and customization.

...

Inkling 2 Mini’s strengths mirror those of Inkling 2 Small: it does best on long-horizon agentic work and is the best among open-weights models of similar size on most tasks we measured.

Inkling 2 Mini scores ahead of every comparable model on agentic coding benchmarks such as DeepSWE v1.1 and SWE-bench Pro v2, and is behind only Qwen3.8-27B on others. On PMPP-Hard, a kernel-optimization benchmark, it approaches the score of the much larger Inkling 2 Small.

While looping improves the model’s reasoning, it doesn’t enable its weights to store more facts—knowledge is mostly a function of total parameter count. Inkling 2 Mini’s score on AA-Omniscience, a measure of factuality, is in line with other models of the same size. Studying the variable-loop model, we saw that performances on long-context benchmarks improve with more passes, such as GraphWalks BFS and MRCR v2; but knowledge-intensive benchmarks doesn’t improve with more passes, such as AA-Omniscience, SimpleQA Verified, SimpleVQA, and WorldVQA.

Inkling 2 Mini overcomes the knowledge gap by efficiently using search and tools. It leads open-weights models of similar size on BrowseComp, DeepSearchQA, and MCP Atlas. It is also strong on knowledge work benchmarks that incorporate search and tool use.

...

Inkling 2 Mini is not the strongest small model for multi-turn chat or for instructions with many constraints: it scores 50.0% on MultiChallenge and 33.4% on ComplexConstraints v1.1, behind Qwen3.8-27B on both. It also trails larger models on reasoning-intensive benchmarks such as CritPt v2 and HLE-Diamond.

signals.title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness adds Strands harness defaults, built-in tools, and lifecycle hooks | Artificial Intelligence
signals.excerpt:
by Evandro Franco, Amir Hegazy, Diego Brasil, and Eshan Kumar on 19 NOV 2026 in Advanced (300), Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Announcements Permalink Share

When building an AI agent, selecting a model is only the first step. The agent still needs tools, instructions for finishing the job, a way to manage context growth in long sessions, and guardrails before it executes any consequential actions, like issuing a refund.

We are upgrading Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness to use Strands harness, our open-source agent harness, released earlier this year, available under an Apache 2.0 license. AgentCore harness also introduces lifecycle hooks, so you can apply your own deterministic checks and notifications at defined points in the agent loop.

With this upgrade, agents that rely on the managed defaults get a recommended model, a task-oriented system prompt, automatic prompt caching (initially for Anthropic models on Amazon Bedrock), and proactive context management. They also get additional built-in tools for planning, web retrieval, filesystem access, context offloading, and task delegation. This gives agents greater capabilities during long tasks, allowing them to keep track of subtasks, reduce context window usage, and delegate work. With hooks, you can transform non-deterministic AI behavior into predictable, safe, and governed workflows by running deterministic code at specific lifecycle checkpoints.

There’s no new resource type or integration to adopt. You automatically get both updates in the AgentCore harness you already use.

...

Strands harness provides an assembled agent foundation with recommended instructions, tools, and context management. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness operates that foundation as a managed AWS service.

...

## A more capable managed harness

Harness now provides a stronger experience when you use its managed defaults:

- A current recommended model. When you omit the model, Harness uses a recommended default model that evolves as new models are released, always keeping your harnesses up to date. Explicit harness-level and per-invocation model configurations continue to take precedence.
- Task-oriented instructions. The managed system prompt encourages the agent to gather relevant context, use appropriate tools, continue until the task is resolved, adapt to failures or denied actions, and verify its work before reporting completion. The default system prompt improves over time to support the latest harness behavior.
- Automatic prompt caching. For supported models using Converse on Amazon Bedrock, Harness caches the system prompt, tool definitions, and conversation history. Repeated calls with the same prompt and tool surface can use lower-priced cache-read tokens, reducing input processing latency and cost.
- Proactive context management. By default, Harness summarizes older conversation turns while retaining recent context once the context window reaches a configurable threshold. Keeping the context lean this way helps Harness run at about 34% lower token cost than other leading harnesses.
- Context offloading. Large tool results can be moved out of the immediate model context. The agent receives a preview and can retrieve the complete result when needed, reducing repeated context usage without losing access to the data.
- Planning across invocations. The `todo_write` tool maintains a structured task plan that can be restored in later invocations within the same session, including after conversation summarization.
- Focused delegation. The `subagent` tool delegates a self-contained task to a fresh worker and returns the result to the parent agent. The worker is internal to the invocation, not a separately managed harness resource, and shares invocation limits and your tool-call lifecycle hooks.
- Web retrieval. The `web_fetch` tool retrieves content from a specified webpage to give your harness up-to-date external context.
- Granular filesystem access. With separate `read`, `write`, and `edit` tools, you can grant only the granular filesystem capabilities an agent needs.

Customer-provided Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, AgentCore Gateway (a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore), Browser, Code Interpreter, inline functions, skills, memory, and customer-provided containers continue to work through the existing harness interfaces.

signals.title: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart now offers a model leaderboard to compare models on quality, speed, and cost - AWS
signals.excerpt:
Posted on: Nov 20, 2026 

Amazon SageMaker JumpStart now offers a model leaderboard in Amazon SageMaker Studio. You can use it to compare foundation models side by side on throughput, latency, and cost, and then deploy or customize the model that fits your workload.

Comparing models has usually meant reading model cards one at a time and relying on benchmark scores that different sources published under different conditions. The JumpStart leaderboard puts consistent measurements in one view. AWS evaluates every model on three reasoning benchmarks, BIG-Bench Hard, GPQA Diamond, and MMLU-Pro, using the same evaluation setup for each model. AWS also measures time to first token, throughput, and instance cost on SageMaker for each JumpStart deployment configuration. You can use all of the filters already available for JumpStart models, such as model provider, license, and input and output modality, to narrow the list. You can also choose a use case profile and an optimization goal (balanced, cost, latency, or throughput) to see the metrics for the configuration you plan to deploy. At launch, the leaderboard covers more than 70 LLMs from providers including Meta, Google, Qwen, IBM, and Arcee.

The JumpStart model leaderboard is available at no additional charge in all AWS commercial Regions where Amazon SageMaker Studio is available. To get started, open SageMaker JumpStart in SageMaker Studio and choose the Leaderboard view. To learn more, see JumpStart leaderboard methodology and read the launch blog post.

signals.title: Cut self-hosted LLM cost and latency with the distributed KV caching agent skill | Artificial Intelligence
signals.excerpt:
by Ravi Yadav, Chaitanya Nuthalapati, and Neeraj Ramachandran on 20 NOV 2026 in Amazon ElastiCache, Expert (400), Technical How-to Permalink Share

Customers increasingly self-host large language models (LLMs) on GPUs for control over cost, accuracy, and latency. However, self-hosting often means paying for redundant GPU work because small, isolated caches on each server can’t hold or share the growing context AI agents and chat applications resend. Consider a legal AI assistant that can accumulate hundreds of thousands of tokens of case history in each conversation. When a lawyer returns to a thread after lunch, responses from the LLM can take minutes. The GPU server that picks up the request has none of that history in its memory. So, the GPU recomputes the key-value (KV) attention states for all of those tokens, a step called prefill, before it writes a word. The same pattern slows down resumed coding agents, agentic AI assistants, and document Q&A assistants. Distributed KV caching with Amazon ElastiCache can cut self-hosted LLM inference costs by up to 40% and time to first token (TTFT) by up to 80%. Distributed KV caching extends GPU-local caches with a shared tier beside your GPU fleet so any server can reuse KV state for days across sessions, routing shifts, and server failures. “ Announcing distributed KV caching for self-hosted LLMs with Amazon ElastiCache” dives into the technical details and the performance benchmarks.

This post details the distributed KV caching skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS. With this skill, you can evaluate and set up distributed KV caching from within your coding agent in a few prompts. The skill guides the agent through checking whether your workload benefits from distributed KV caching, setting up a cache cluster for testing or production workload, and troubleshooting your LLM inference caching. The skill works with Kiro, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and other coding agents that support Agent Skills. We walk through how the skill works with four conversations: diagnosing a slow first token, sizing and pricing the cache, setting it up, and fixing a failed transfer.

## Why a skill for KV caching and what can it do?

The benefits for your workload depend on characteristics such as LLM models used, user traffic patterns, and prompt routing choices, and can be complex to estimate. We created the KVTrace tool to get close estimates of the benefits for your workload, from your own model and traffic before you deploy any infrastructure, at no additional charge. The skill simplifies this evaluation and the setup, and guides your coding agent through the following best practices before changing anything:

- A fit check before any spend. The agent reads your GPU fleet with a read-only `describe-instances` call and counts Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) interfaces. It asks only for what it can’t see: engine, model, tensor-parallel (TP) size, KV data type, server price, and how often prompts repeat. It stops and explains when something doesn’t fit.
- Numbers from your workload. For short prompts, loading KV state can take longer than computing it again. Above a certain prompt length (the cutover point), the read wins. That cutover and how often your prompts repeat decide whether the cache is worth its price. The agent estimates savings from your own traffic with KVTrace, at no additional charge, and stops if they don’t cover the cache’s cost. Every number says where it came from.
- Manage configuration across inference servers with the stack you already run. The agent adds the LMCache connector to your existing vLLM or SGLang engine, including vLLM workers under serving frameworks such as llm-d and Ray Serve. It keeps your routing and the engine’s settings and sets the servers in your inference fleet to one KV ID mechanism (hash and seed) and an explicit KV data type. Matching settings avoid key mismatches, where each server writes KV state the others can’t find.
- Implements best practices. Before production traffic, the agent empties the local tiers and checks that two cache-loaded runs give the same output, because a layout mismatch can produce healthy hit counters and wrong answers. The skill guides the agent to seek explicit approval for high-impact operations such as creating, changing, or deleting resources.

## Prerequisites

These flows, from estimating benefits to setup, require the following:

- A coding agent that supports Agent Skills, such as Kiro or Claude Code.
- GPU instances that support EFA RDMA write, such as p5.
- LMCache 0.5.8rc1 or later and vLLM 0.11.1 or later (SGLang 0.5.13 or later).
- ElastiCache for Valkey 9.1 or later, on cache.i8ge.48xlarge nodes (if setting up the cache).

...

## Flow 2: Estimating savings

To size the savings, we gave the agent an example fleet of 8 p5 instances that serve 64,000-token prompts for a multi-turn retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assistant. The agent looked up the GPU and cache node prices and derived the prefill rate and KV size from benchmarks. Finally, the agent recommended two cache.i8ge.48xlarge nodes for distributed KV caching. The following figure shows the agent’s summary and the inputs it used.

Figure 2: The agent’s summary and inputs. It looked up both prices in the AWS price list and explains how it arrived at the recompute figure

We didn’t provide a cache hit rate, which is the share of recomputed tokens the cache would serve. The agent therefore presents scenarios and recommends a KVTrace run to identify the cache hit rate. KVTrace records the KV cache events from vLLM or SGLang. It then replays them offline against a shared KV cache of each candidate size. The recorder never writes token IDs or prompt text. Traces hold block hashes and token counts. Block hashes come from token content, so pass `--anonymize-key-file` when your prompts are sensitive. The skill records on every GPU server for a representative window, such as a full business day. The agent also notes that freed GPU time turns into dollars only if you run fewer servers or serve more traffic on the same ones.

Figure 3: The top of a KVTrace report from synthetic demo traffic. It recommends the smallest capacity that reaches 90% of the savings ceiling.

## Flow 3: Setting up a distributed KV cache

We prompted the agent with: “Set up a shared L2 KV cache for LLM inference, starting from scratch.” Before it creates anything, the agent requests your confirmation to set up the suggested cache node count in your Availability Zone, at the estimated price. Once confirmed, it creates the right security group with EFA permissions, and a Valkey 9.1 cluster that uses a custom parameter group with caching eviction policies. LMCache gets its own cache user, with the password in AWS Secrets Manager. The agent prepares the GPU servers and starts one LMCache server per GPU server. Then it checks the cluster with a small test object and confirms that repeated prompts load their KV state from the cache over Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA). On a GPU fleet, the skill checks the measured L2 share against the KVTrace prediction. For the full setup with every command, see Getting started with distributed KV caching in the Amazon ElastiCache documentation.

signals.title: Saturn Cloud Brings Tileward's Compressed Models to Its Token Factory, Turning the Same GPUs Into More Tokens
signals.excerpt:
Nov 20, 2026, 13:00 ET

Tileward's compressed open models free up GPU memory, so operators on Saturn Cloud's token factory platform can serve more tokens from the GPUs they already own, with no change to their serving stack or rate cards.

NEW YORK, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Saturn Cloud, the inference platform for enterprises running open models, today announced a partnership with Tileward to bring its compressed open models to Saturn Cloud's token factory platform. Operators can run the same models with less GPU memory, so each GPU can serve more tokens.

Saturn Cloud's token factory turns GPU fleets into managed inference and fine-tuning services that operators sell to their own customers, under their own brand. Tenant isolation, quotas, metering, and enterprise governance are built in. It runs on NVIDIA Dynamo, in public cloud, private cloud, or on-premises. Serving Kimi K3 to 16 live agent sessions on NVIDIA GB300 GPUs, Saturn Cloud delivered 7,380 total tokens per second per GPU at about 37 tokens per second per user, matching the SemiAnalysis InferenceX benchmark recipe on the same GPUs. Tileward's models run on this serving stack.

"Operators sell inference from GPUs they've already paid for, and memory is usually what runs out first," said Sebastian Metti, Founder and CEO of Saturn Cloud. "Tileward gives that memory back, so operators can take on more customers and longer contexts with the fleet they have, without buying more GPUs."

Tileward, a member of the NVIDIA Inception program for startups, offers compressed models that are up to 78% smaller than the published weights. Tileward evaluates each one against the original on benchmarks including MMLU, SWE-bench Verified, and AgentBench.

"Making a model smaller was never the hard part. Proving it still gives the right answers is," said Anantha Sharma, Founder and CTO of Tileward. "We publish how we measure every model, so operators on Saturn Cloud can check the quality before they sell a single token of it."

Operators can swap in Tileward's weights for the published ones, and their serving stack, tenants, rate cards, and brand stay the same. The freed memory lets them run more copies of each model, fit large models on fewer GPUs, and serve more concurrent users with longer contexts. Serving more tokens from each GPU lowers the cost per token, giving operators more margin on input, cached, and output rates, or room to price lower.

Available Now on Saturn Cloud

Compressed versions of gpt-oss-120b, GLM-5.3, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash are available now to neoclouds, AI factory operators, telcos, sovereign AI providers, and enterprises running Saturn Cloud's token factory platform on their own GPUs. Contact Saturn Cloud or Tileward to add them to a deployment.

signals.title: Gemini API tool retrieval for efficient agent scaling
signals.excerpt:
Nov 19, 2026

 Tool Retrieval is now in preview in the Gemini Interactions API. Load tool parameter schemas on demand instead of sending your full tool library in every prompt,designed to reduce input tokens and keep tool selection accurate as your agent scales. 

Lucia Loher

Product Manager, Gemini API

Nora Kassner

Research Scientist, Google DeepMind

 

Today we're launching Tool Retrieval in the Gemini API, available in preview in the Interactions API.

When an agent connects to dozens or even hundreds of tools, sending every full parameter schema on every request adds up fast. It inflates input token counts, adds latency, and lowers tool-selection accuracy as the candidate list grows. Tool Retrieval lets your agent keep its full tool library on standby and load parameter schemas only when the current task needs them.

## How it works

To turn on Tool Retrieval, add a `tool_search` tool to your request and set `defer_loading: true` on the tools you want to hold back. The model still sees the name and description of every deferred tool, so it knows what's available, but the parameter schemas stay out of context. When the model needs a tool, it asks for it by name, the API loads the full schema, and the model calls the function, all inside the same request.

...

There's no index to build or host. Gemini runs the search on the server, so the only changes to your code are the new tool and a flag on the tools you want to defer. You can keep your most-used tools loaded up front and defer the long tail.

Tool Retrieval also plays well with prefix caching. Deferred schemas stay out of the start of the prompt, and the schemas the model loads are added later in the conversation, so the cached prefix stays the same from turn to turn.

Tool Retrieval also works with remote MCP servers in the Gemini API. Set `defer_loading: true` on an `mcp_server` tool and every tool that server exposes is loaded on demand, so you can connect a large server without listing its tools one by one.

## How client-side retrieval works

If you maintain your own tool registry, embedding index, or per-user permission filter, declare the `tool_search` with `"execution": "client"` and define your search parameters. Client-side retrieval adds one round trip per search, because your app runs the lookup.

...

## How pricing and supported models work

Tool Retrieval has no separate charge. Input and output tokens are billed at the standard rates for the model you call. Turning on `tool_search` adds a small, fixed block of input tokens, and each schema the model loads is billed as input for the rest of the conversation, the same as a tool declared up front. You save tokens when the schemas you never load outweigh the ones you do, which is the usual case for large libraries. Measure it against your own traffic.

Tool Retrieval works with Gemini 3.6 and later models, including all Gemini 4 models, in the Interactions API.

signals.title: Optimizing DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash PD & Colocate Serving on H20-3e - LMSYS Org
signals.excerpt:
Siyuan Chen, Bingjia Wang, Bofeng Jiang, Yongxu Ai, and Kaixin Shen — Ant International AI Infra Team November 19, 2026

...

## Overview

We optimized disaggregated DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash serving on H20-3e by tuning prefill and decode parallelism, supporting BCG with prefill CP and bounded SWA replay, and speeding up Indexer kernels. Compared with TP4, the final configuration cut mean end-to-end latency by 65.5% and delivered 2.91× the output throughput.

Our intra-node PD deployment used four GPUs each for prefill and decode, with KV cache transfers over NVLink. Mean end-to-end latency fell from 13.63 s to 4.70 s, and output throughput rose from 847 to 2,465 tokens/s. Prefill context parallelism paired with decode data parallelism gave the largest gain, followed by FP8 DeepGEMM scoring.

| Cumulative configuration | Mean E2E (ms) | Output (tok/s) | Mean TTFT (ms) | Mean TPOT (ms) | P99 E2E (ms) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| TP4 baseline | 13,633.80 | 846.76 | 12,037.73 | 3.20 | 21,306.70 |
| 1. Prefill CP + decode DP | 7,547.46 (−44.64%) | 1,537.90 | 5,156.84 (-57%) | 4.79 | 14,012.91 |
| 2. FP8 DeepGEMM | 5,294.89 (−29.85%) | 2,200.82 | 2,662.13 (-48%) | 5.28 | 11,016.82 |
| 3. Breakable CUDA Graphs | 5,100.87 (−3.66%) | 2,290.05 | 2,390.32 (-10%) | 5.43 | 10,641.21 |
| 4. TP MoE | 4,811.81 (−5.67%) | 2,425.96 | 1,877.23 (-22%) | 5.88 | 10,224.78 |
| 5. Larger prefill score tiles | 4,773.97 (−0.79%) | 2,450.67 | 1,838.15 (-2%) | 5.88 | 10,284.72 |
| 6. Prefill selection fusion | 4,774.47 (+0.01%) | 2,440.68 | 1,802.77 (-2%) | 5.96 | 10,221.00 |
| 7. Paged K-tile reuse | 4,698.65 (−1.59%) | 2,464.90 | 1,894.54 | 5.62 (-6%) | 10,073.00 |

Most of the latency gain came before the first token. Mean time to first token (TTFT) fell from 12.04 s to 1.89 s. Mean time per output token after the first (TPOT) rose from 3.20 to 5.62 ms. At fixed concurrency, faster prefill can keep decode busier, and faster decode can free client slots for new prompts. That can shift queueing between the two workers.

In the original sweep, the median prefill queue fell from 15 requests at baseline to 9 after CP and DP, then to 4 after DeepGEMM and 3 after breakable graphs. It reached zero with TP MoE. The median decode queue stayed at zero.

## Measurement Setup

The router sends each request through prefill and decode. The workers transfer the KV state directly over intra-node Mooncake NVLink. The baseline runs TP4 attention and EP4 MoE on both workers with eager BF16 Torch prefill scoring. All runs used the same DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash checkpoint, Humming W4A8 MoE, a DSpark block size of 5, and 8,192-token prefill chunks.

| Workload | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Requests and concurrency | 256 requests, 24 in flight |
| Nominal input | 61,440 shared tokens + 4,096 request-specific tokens |
| Output | 500 tokens per request |
| Cache protocol | 10 warmup requests, then a cache flush before measurement |
| Observed cache hit rate | 93.21% |

All 256 requests completed and produced 128,000 output tokens in each run. The TP4 baseline and Steps 1–3 are single runs from the original sweep. Steps 4–7 show the mean of all completed follow-up runs for each configuration. The E2E percentages compare adjacent rows. P99 is calculated per run and then averaged.

...

## 2. FP8 DeepGEMM for the Prefill Indexer

The Indexer scores visible keys before selecting a small subset for attention. On Hopper, we gather each request’s packed FP4 keys once, convert queries and keys to FP8 E4M3, and call DeepGEMM’s `fp8_mqa_logits` in each prefill Indexer layer. Each query can still see only the keys allowed by its causal mask and candidate set.

The queries are already FP4 fake-quantized, so we cast them to E4M3 without applying another scale. For keys, we apply the FP4 block’s power-of-two scale in FP32 and clamp to −448 to +448 before casting. This keeps out-of-range values finite. DeepGEMM gets unit key scales because the block scales are already applied.

The power-of-two scaling preserves exactly representable values. Out-of-range keys saturate, very small values can round or underflow, and the change in scoring precision can affect rankings. In a separate prefill probe on a 64K prompt, we sampled 64 query rows across 8 Indexer layers. None of the 16,774,528 sampled key values needed clamping. The BF16 and DeepGEMM scorers shared 99.08% of the selected top-k entries on those same rows.

Serving result. Mean E2E went from 7,547.46 to 5,294.89 ms (−29.85%). Output throughput rose from 1,537.90 to 2,200.82 tokens/s (+43.11%). SGLang PR #49066

...

## 8. Colocate Serving Optimization

We ran the same request workload at concurrency 24 on a single four-GPU worker with DSpark. Compared with the BF16 TP4 baseline, mean E2E fell from 18.62 s to 7.96 s (57.26% lower), and output throughput rose from 642 to 1,483 tokens/s (130.79% higher).

| Cumulative configuration | Mean E2E (ms) | Output (tok/s) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| TP baseline (BF16 prefill Indexer) | 18,619.53 | 642.46 |
| Prefill CP, decode TP (BF16 prefill Indexer) | 12,499.25 (-33%) | 949.97 |
| FP8 DeepGEMM | 9,727.21 (-22%) | 1,222.38 |
| Breakable CUDA Graphs | 9,418.85 (-3%) | 1,256.71 |
| Paged K-tile reuse | 8,694.89 (-8%) | 1,367.96 |
| Tensor-parallel MoE | 8,632.46 (-1%) | 1,377.49 |
| Batch-wise prefill CP and decode DP | 7,957.13 (-8%) | 1,482.72 |

We added batch-wise prefill CP and decode DP to the same worker. Prefill still splits prompt tokens across four ranks. During decode and target verification, each rank instead handles a slice of the batches with all attention heads, and the worker gathers the results back into batch order.

Adding decode DP to the prefill CP configuration cut mean E2E by 7.82% and raised output throughput by 7.64%. Decode DP requires replicated KV and Indexer keys. With the same `--max-running-requests 64`, the startup log reported 955,136 KV token slots with decode TP and 953,088 with decode DP. Those counts measure the KV pool. The supported concurrency also depends on the length of live sequences. SGLang PR #45729

For this workload, the colocated configuration produced more output tokens per second per GPU (371 vs. 308). The eight-GPU PD configuration delivered lower mean latency (4.70 vs. 7.96 s) and higher total throughput.

Nov 19, 2026

## Highlights

- First HIP EP integration: FastFlow v1.0.13 brings HIP EP v0.5.3 into FLM through the new oga-hipep backend.
- Two flows, one umbrella: NPU and GPU execution now sit behind the same CLI, local API, and conversation format.

The iGPU flow powered by HIP EP in FastFlow v1.0.13 is an early access release, now available for wider adoption and feedback. Features, performance, and supported configurations may change as we learn from your use. Please share your feedback through the FastFlow repository.

Today, FastFlow takes a big step forward. With v1.0.13, released on November 13, 2026, it brings two inference flows under one umbrella: the NPU path developers already know, and a new high-performance GPU path powered by HIP EP. One single local API and CLI. More ways to run AI on AMD hardware.

FastFlow is a lightweight runtime of about 17 MB for AMD Ryzen™ AI systems. It offers a single-command CLI and an OpenAI-compatible server, so existing tools and applications connect without rewriting. On Ryzen AI NPUs, it demonstrates strong throughput and power efficiency. Now the GPU joins the party.

## Meet HIP EP

HIP EP is an open-source ONNX Runtime execution provider built for performance on AMD GPUs. It compiles an ONNX graph through an MLIR pipeline and runs it with hipBLASLt and custom HIP kernels. As highlighted in the HIP EP site , it supports more than 20 model architectures and context lengths up to 128K tokens on the Ryzen AI Max, Ryzen AI 400, and Ryzen AI 300 series. FastFlow now brings the GPU performance to everyday developers through the `oga-hipep` backend, built on ONNX Runtime GenAI. The code and releases are in the HIP EP repository.

HIP EP's benchmark tracking on a Ryzen™ AI Max (Strix Halo) system shows the latest build ahead of llama.cpp (Vulkan) at 16K context. Time to first token (TTFT) is about 43% lower and decode throughput (TPS) is about 7% higher. The table shows results normalized to llama.cpp (Vulkan) as 1.00.

signals.title: FlashInfer on ROCm routes AMD GPU kernels automatically | AI.info
signals.excerpt:
AI.info Team · · fact-checked · against 1 source ↓ · Published 20 Nov 2026

FlashInfer on ROCm now selects between AMD's AITER library and in-tree HIP kernels for supported attention calls, using a default automatic backend. The release, described in an AMD blog post on November 20, also adds FP8 prefill, fused mixture-of-experts operations and AITER decode under CUDA graph capture.

FlashInfer is an open-source library of attention and large language model serving kernels. The ROCm release supports AMD Instinct MI300X, MI325X, MI350X and MI355X GPUs. Its decode, prefill and multi-head latent attention (MLA) wrappers retain the signatures and argument order of upstream FlashInfer v0.6.18.

## How routing works

Single, batch paged and batch ragged prefill, as well as batch decode, have both AITER and in-tree HIP backends. For attention calls, the automatic setting first checks whether AITER can handle the data types, key-value cache layout, masks and head dimensions, then applies architecture-specific routing rules.

AMD says those rules follow its testing and benchmarking on CDNA3 and CDNA4 GPUs. The in-tree path handles calls that AITER cannot serve, including an FP8 key-value cache read by a 16-bit query and batch decode using tensor cores.

MLA and fused mixture-of-experts operations use AITER only. Normalization, activation, rotary position embedding and key-value cache append operations use in-tree kernels by default, with AITER available as an opt-in for some entry points.

After planning a batch prefill or batch decode call, the wrapper reports the selected backend and, for most AITER declines, the reason for the fallback. AITER attention kernels are launched from FlashInfer's C++ code; MLA remains an exception that runs AITER through Python.

## New operations and limits

The release also brings cascade attention, MLA and standalone rotary position embedding operations that were in progress in the preceding prefill-attention release. POD-Attention overlaps prefill and decode in one kernel.

The fused mixture-of-experts operation supports bf16 and fp16, as well as FP8 expert weights. Each expert weight must first be pre-shuffled, following quantization for FP8 weights.

The in-tree FP8 key-value cache kernels use FNUZ encodings on both supported architectures and refuse OCP encodings. On gfx950, a cache written in float8_e4m3fn for AITER FP8 prefill cannot also be read by decode: the in-tree decode rejects that encoding, while AITER decode accepts only 16-bit key-value caches.

Some upstream modules are not supported on ROCm because they wrap CUDA-only libraries or other CUDA-specific components. Other operations, including flashinfer.topk and the selective state update in flashinfer.mamba, do not have a ROCm implementation.

...

The supported configuration uses ROCm 10.1.0, PyTorch 2.12.0, Python 3.12, Ubuntu 24.04 and amd-aiter 0.1.21.post2 built from source. No wheel or prebuilt image is published for the release, so FlashInfer on ROCm must be built from the repository.

signals.title: NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin Leads MLPerf Training and Agentic Inference Tests
signals.excerpt:
NVIDIA has introduced its Vera Rubin NVL72 platform in the latest MLPerf results, claiming leadership across AI training, post-training and agentic inference. The debut gives the company another strong performance story as AI developers move from training large models toward serving agents that reason, call tools and maintain long-running context.

In MLPerf Training v6.1, NVIDIA platforms held the fastest result on all seven benchmarks, while Vera Rubin delivered the fastest time on six. In its first MLPerf Endpoints submission, Vera Rubin also reported more than 10 times the throughput per kilowatt of the previous-generation GB300 NVL72 on a Kimi K3 agentic workload at a shared responsiveness threshold. The Endpoints figures for Vera Rubin remain provisional and pending MLCommons verification.

The results come entirely from NVIDIA’s own blog and developer documentation. They are based on published MLPerf entries, but the interpretation of the gains, the software maturity claims and references to customer value are vendor-reported. That distinction matters for buyers comparing platforms, especially because the Vera Rubin submissions use different accelerator counts and configurations from some GB300 comparisons.

## Vera Rubin’s debut across training workloads

NVIDIA says Vera Rubin NVL72 achieved up to twice the performance per GPU of an optimized GB300 NVL72 baseline in MLPerf Training v6.1. The suite spans language models, image generation, recommendation systems and reinforcement-learning post-training, making the result broader than a single large-language-model comparison.

The largest training improvement came on the DeepSeek-V3 671B Mixture-of-Experts benchmark. Vera Rubin completed the workload in 4.14 minutes on 1,024 GPUs, compared with 8.03 minutes for GB300 NVL72 at the same scale, according to NVIDIA’s account of the MLPerf data. Vera Rubin also maintained more than 97% scaling efficiency as the run expanded from 256 to 1,024 GPUs.

NVIDIA’s platforms together produced the fastest absolute result on every benchmark, but the distinction between platforms is important. GB300 NVL72 achieved the fastest absolute DeepSeek-V3 result in the round by running on 10,240 GPUs, completing the job in 1.38 minutes. Vera Rubin’s strongest comparison is therefore its performance at the same 1,024-GPU scale, not an across-the-board replacement of the largest GB300 installation.

The new Qwen 3.5 397B GRPO benchmark also puts attention on post-training. Vera Rubin NVL72 completed it in 10.44 minutes on 1,024 GPUs, compared with 13.78 minutes for GB300 NVL72 at the same scale. NVIDIA submitted Vera Rubin with both TensorRT-LLM and vLLM inference backends, reporting times of 10.44 and 10.94 minutes respectively.

That workload is relevant to agent development because reinforcement-learning post-training repeatedly generates rollouts, scores them and updates model weights. NVIDIA says the Vera CPU portion of the system supported more than 22,500 concurrent reinforcement-learning environments across 256 CPUs in one rack, although the source does not provide an independent validation of that operational claim.

## Agentic inference claims remain provisional

MLPerf Endpoints v1.0 evaluates inference through coding and enterprise workflows rather than measuring token generation in isolation. The test tracks responsiveness while agents generate tool calls and complete tasks, with separate SWE-bench Verified evaluations used to assess end-to-end task solving.

NVIDIA’s provisional Vera Rubin results cover Kimi K3, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. Across those models, the company reports five- to 10-times higher throughput per kilowatt and three- to five-times higher end-to-end interactivity at matched concurrency compared with GB300 NVL72.

The headline comparison is the Kimi K3 result. At a shared minimum end-to-end interactivity of 50 tokens per second per user, NVIDIA reports more than 10 times the throughput per kilowatt for Vera Rubin. The cited MLPerf entry used 32 Vera Rubin accelerators and 48 GB300 accelerators, so the result demonstrates system efficiency under the published test conditions rather than a simple one-for-one chip comparison.

The Vera Rubin result is also provisional. NVIDIA’s technical post says the submission is pending MLCommons Association verification and may change during peer review. The corresponding GB300 result is identified as verified. For enterprise buyers, that status makes the result useful as an early signal, but not yet equivalent to a fully verified benchmark record.

signals.excerpt:
November 20, 2026

...

Introducing MedChemBench, a benchmark that tests how well AI models read molecular structures, interpret experimental results, and choose which compounds to test next.

...

We’re introducing MedChemBench, a benchmark that evaluates AI models on reasoning tasks drawn from medicinal chemistry research. It tests whether models can connect a molecule’s structure with experimental evidence to explain results, compare compounds, and predict their properties. Building AI that can reliably support this work is one step towards helping scientists develop better medicines.

...

MedChemBench measures these abilities through 99 problems drawn from published research. At the xhigh reasoning setting, GPT‑6.2 Astra earned 84.5% of the available credit, compared with 83.3% for GPT‑6 Astra, 82.0% for GPT‑6.1 Sol, and 58.2% for GPT‑5.6 Sol. GPT‑6 Astra was strongest at reconstructing molecular structures and explaining experimental evidence. Selecting compounds and predicting their numerical properties proved harder for that model.

## What MedChemBench grades

MedChemBench draws on 117 papers and patents and includes 761 distinct molecular structures. For most problems, models receive the context available at a chosen point in a research program: the biological target, the researchers’ goals, the compounds studied so far, and selected experimental findings.

The benchmark evaluates four components:

- Molecular structures. Correct atom connections and specified stereochemistry in molecules assembled from the drawings and chemical groups provided.
- Scientific reasoning. Explanations supported by the supplied evidence, such as the reasons for choosing one compound over another.
- Ranking and selection. Compound rankings and choices that meet the stated requirements.
- Property predictions. Agreement with the numerical values and categories reported in the source material, including measured and calculated molecular properties.

...

These results do not establish whether models can discover new drugs or improve laboratory decisions. Prior exposure to the published sources cannot be ruled out, and each response was a single attempt without tools, feedback, or new experiments.

signals.title: NVIDIA AI Releases Nemotron-Labs-Sigma, a Continuous Diffusion Language Model with 14 checkpoints at 3B/8B - MarkTechPost
signals.excerpt:
November 20, 2026

NVIDIA has released Nemotron-Labs-Sigma, a collection of 14 open checkpoints at 3B and 8B scale. Nemotron-Labs-Sigma is a continuous diffusion language model family that denoises text in a 16-D embedding space. Most diffusion LLMs, such as LLaDA and Dream, work on discrete tokens. Sigma works in a smooth latent space instead. NVIDIA team states that this makes few-step distillation and trajectory steering practical for text. 

## TL;DR

- Size: 3B and 8B parameters, 14 checkpoints. Context is 4,096 tokens (8,192 for Sigma-8B-instruct).
- Runs on: 1 NVIDIA GPU in bfloat16 (Ampere, Lovelace, Hopper, Blackwell). About 120 to 140 tokens/s on 1 H100. No CPU support, no quantized variants listed.
- Performance: Sigma-8B base averages 71.16 on NVIDIA’s 6-task suite, ahead of NLD-8B (70.22).
- Best: 91.96 on GSM8K (Sigma-8B-instruct, 256 DDPM steps).
- Worst: 17.00 on AIME25 (same model and sampler).
- Bottom line: Best: the 8-step distilled 8B keeps a 70.34 average. Worst: the instruct average (59.14) trails NLD-8B (59.92).

...

Each token maps to a point in a learned 16-D embedding space. Training adds Gaussian noise to these embeddings and teaches the model to remove it. The embedding geometry is learned jointly with the denoiser.

Generation runs blockwise. Each denoised block is committed to a KV cache before the next starts. Blocks default to 64 tokens.

...

## How does Sigma perform on benchmarks?

On the research’s 6-task base suite, Sigma-8B with 256 DDPM steps averages 71.16. NLD-8B in diffusion mode scores 70.22, Dream-7B 58.74 and LLaDA-8B 41.78. Qwen3-8B in AR mode scores 68.91. A cheaper 32-step DDIM sampler still gives Sigma-8B a 70.18 average.

Coding is the standout. Sigma-8B scores 65.12 on HumanEval versus 62.80 for NLD-8B. MBPP is weaker, at 65.74 versus 67.00.

After SFT, Sigma-8B-instruct scores 91.96 on GSM8K, 78.40 on MATH-500 and 82.50 on HumanEval. Hard reasoning stays limited, at 23.33 on AIME24 and 17.00 on AIME25. Its 10-task average of 59.14 sits just below NLD-8B at 59.92. All scores are NVIDIA’s own evaluations.

## How fast are the distilled and speculative checkpoints?

Sigma-distill-8B-nfe8 decodes each 32-token block in 8 denoiser calls plus 1 readout. Its card reports a 6-task mean of 70.34, with 88.44 on GSM8K and 65.18 on HumanEval. That is close to the 256-step teacher.

NVIDIA’s launch thread frames the gain as 8 tokens per forward on math and 4 on code.

The distill-spec checkpoints add self-speculative decoding. A diffusion head drafts a 32-token block, and the model’s own AR head verifies it. Output exactly matches greedy AR decoding. On 1 GB200 with SGLang, the 8B spec model runs 3.46x faster than AR decoding on average. NLD-8B reaches 3.04x on the same setup. Peak speedups reach 4.20x at 8B and 3.18x at 3B.

## How do you deploy Nemotron-Labs-Sigma?

All 14 checkpoints are on Hugging Face under the NVIDIA Nemotron Open Model License. The cards state the models are ready for commercial use. You need a CUDA GPU in bfloat16: Ampere, Lovelace, Hopper or Blackwell. CPU inference is not supported.

Loading needs PyTorch 2.4+, Transformers 4.55+ and `trust_remote_code`. On 1 H100, the base model generates about 120 to 140 tokens/s. The distilled card lists vLLM, SGLang and Docker Model Runner for serving. NVIDIA hosts no API.

signals.excerpt:
###### The Linux Foundation | 19 November 2026

Distributed KV Caching Maximizes GPU Servers and Minimizes Costs

Agentic AI applications waste expensive GPU compute by constantly reprocessing the same prompt instructions, tool definitions, and conversation history. Released alongside Valkey 9.2, open source distributed KV caching enhances AI workload efficiency by creating a large, shared cache across a GPU fleet, allowing inference engines to reuse computed work rather than recomputing. Builders running open-weight models on self-managed inference can now connect a distributed KV cache through LMCache, which plugs into engines like vLLM and SGLang using a single configuration change. Distributed KV caching achieves:

- Lower AI inference spend: Reduces costs by up to 40% by allowing teams to serve more users on the GPUs they already have.
- Improved latency: Decreases time-to-first-token by up to 80%.
- Seamless deployment, no vendor-lock in: Works on any cloud or infrastructure with zero application code updates.

## Path Hash Makes Finding AI Context More Efficient

While distributed KV caching saves expensive compute, efficiently locating that shared context has traditionally required engineering teams to build and maintain complex, custom lookup logic.
